source_text: Usque ad legem enim peccatum in hoc mundo; peccatum autem non imputabatur, cum lex non esset, sed regnavit mors ab Adam usque ad Moysen etiam in eos, qui non peccaverunt in similitudine praevaricationis Adae, qui est forma futuri [n296] . Qualitatem peccati appellationum varietate discernit, ut aliud ostendat esse peccatum, aliud praevaricationem; vultque in hoc dumtaxat loco omnem quidem praevaricationem peccatum videri, non omne autem peccatum praevaricationem, ut per vocabulum praevaricationis peccato crescat invidia magisque rei esse videantur, qui fuerint praecepta transgressi, quam qui sine legis admonitione rationis ingenitae dissimulatione deliquerint. Ante eam ergo legem, quae per Moysen data est et consignata litteris, cuius sanctione actuum forma praescripta est, quam ignorare populo sub ea degenti non licuit, medium illud tempus inter Adam et Moysen, mortales varia studiorum pravitate pollutos, peccati Apostolus, non praevaricationis accusat.
pass_a_gloss: For until the law sin in this world; but sin was not being imputed, when the law was not, but death reigned from Adam until Moses even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression, who is a form of the one to come. He discerns the quality of sin by a variety of appellations, so that he may show that one thing is sin, another transgression; and he wants in this place at any rate that every transgression indeed seem a sin, but not every sin a transgression, so that through the vocabulary of transgression envy may grow for sin and those may seem more defendants who shall have transgressed precepts than those who without a warning of the law have offended by a dissembling of inborn reason. Before that law therefore which was given through Moses and sealed by letters, by whose sanction a form of acts was prescribed, which it was not allowed a people living under it to ignore, that middle time between Adam and Moses, mortals polluted by a varied crookedness of pursuits, the Apostle accuses of sin, not of transgression.

pass_b_english: ‘For until the law, sin was in this world; but sin was not imputed when there was no law. Yet death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a figure of the one to come’ (Romans 5:13–14). Through different terms he distinguishes kinds of sin, showing that sin is one thing and transgression another. At least in this passage, he intends every transgression to be regarded as sin, but not every sin as transgression. The term ‘transgression’ increases the odium of sin, so that those who crossed a command appear more guilty than those who sinned without the law’s warning by disregarding their inborn reason. Therefore, before the law given through Moses and committed to writing—whose enactment prescribed a pattern of conduct that people living under it were not permitted to ignore—the apostle accuses mortals stained with various forms of corrupt activity of sin, not transgression: those living in the interval between Adam and Moses.

choices.why: Adam's act of crossing the command; Julian's example of sin, not a transmitted nature.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
